newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Air Force chief to quit in apparent protest.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Air Force chief to quit in apparent protest.

text.p: The U.S. Air Force's top general announced his resignation on Monday, apparently to protest against the possible blaming of subordinates for security lapses that let guerrillas kill 19 airmen.
Gen. Ronald Fogleman, the U.S. Air Force chief of staff, requested early retirement, effective on Sept. 1 or before.

In a statement released by the Air Force, he said he was acting to "defuse the perceived confrontation" between him and Defence Secretary William Cohen over the truck bombing last year of the service's Khobar Towers barracks in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia.
Cohen is expected to decide this week whether to hold one or more commanders responsible for failing to take steps that might have thwarted the attack on June 25, 1996.

A Pentagon task force last year faulted Air Force field commanders for not paying adequate attention to security around the Khobar barracks. Fogleman, 55, was known to consider the criticism unfair second-guessing.
Without spelling out his stance on apportioning blame, he said on Monday his sense of loyalty to subordinates had led him to conclude "I may be out of step" with his superiors.
"I do not want the institution to suffer, and I am afraid it will if I am seen as a divisive force and not a team player," he said, referring to the Air Force.
Cohen praised Fogleman in a statement for serving his country with "courage, vision and distinction" during a 34-year military career that included 315 combat missions as a fighter pilot.
"I respect Gen. Fogleman's personal decision to retire to pursue new opportunities after his service to the Air Force and to the nation," he said.

President Bill Clinton in a statement said Fogleman's "leadership and wise counsel will be truly missed in the senior decision-making ranks of our national security structure." Fogleman was a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Appointed to the Air Force's top uniformed job in 1994, Fogleman will be the service's first chief of staff to step down voluntarily or in protest before completing his four-year term.

In 1995 he became known as the "accountability general" after grounding five officers for their role in shooting down two U.S. Army Blackhawk helicopters over Iraq. Twenty-six people were killed when U.S. pilots monitoring the "no-fly zone" after the Gulf War downed the helicopters, which were on a diplomatic mission.

Fogleman held that military commanders should be held accountable when they erred but backed up when that was appropriate, Cable News Network reported after an off-camera interview with him on Monday.
"And he thinks that the Air Force officers there (in Saudi Arabia) did everything they reasonably could," the CNN correspondent said.

A Pentagon task force found last September that commanders of U.S. air operations in Saudi Arabia at the time of the bombing "did not take all measures possible to protect the forces at Khobar Towers."
The task force, headed by retired Army Gen. Wayne Downing, recommended that punitive action be considered by the chain of command -- ultimately by the defence secretary.

The Air Force said in January it had delayed promoting Brig. Gen. Terryl Schwalier, who had overall command of U.S. air operations in Saudi Arabia, to major general pending final action in the controversy.
CNN said Fogleman wanted Schwalier to be given his second general's star. Before the delay, Schwalier had been nominated for promotion by Clinton and confirmed by the Senate.
